title: The Women of Dharasana
subtitle: Sarojini Naidu and the Salt that Stung an Empire
moral: Courage can turn suffering into witness.

sources.citation: Webb Miller, United Press eyewitness dispatch from Dharasana, 21 May 1930
sources.note: Contemporary global press account of the lathi charge.

sources.citation: United States Senate Congressional Record, May 1930, reading of Miller's dispatch
Geraldine Forbes, Women in Modern India (Cambridge, 1996)
sources.note: Modern analysis of women's participation in Civil Disobedience.

panels.shot: low-angle mid-shot of Sarojini Naidu at the head of a silent column of satyagrahis, distant salt pans glimmering in harsh sun, armed policemen faint on the horizon

dialogue.text: May 1930: with Gandhi in prison, it is Sarojini Naidu who walks unarmed towards Dharasana, where lathis, salt, and the world’s press will collide.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Sarojini Naidu seated by lamplight, reading a telegram, shadows long on the mud floor

dialogue.text: On the night of 4 May 1930, news moves faster than the trains: Gandhi has been arrested on the march to the sea. The salt satyagraha leader is gone.

panels.shot: medium shot, profile, Sarojini rising, others’ silhouettes in the doorway behind her

dialogue.speaker: sarojini_naidu
dialogue.text: They have taken Bapu. The road to Dharasana is now ours.

panels.shot: wide shot of an improvised meeting under a tree, Sarojini addressing men and women seated on the ground

dialogue.text: Abbas Tyabji, the old judge turned rebel, is arrested next. The British hope Dharasana will fall silent. Instead, the Congress turns to the Nightingale of India.

panels.shot: close-up on Sarojini’s face as she speaks, eyes steady, a notebook with Gandhi’s instructions visible in her hand

dialogue.speaker: sarojini_naidu
dialogue.text: You will not raise a hand in anger. Your courage will be your only shield.

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot of training: rows of satyagrahis sitting, then standing, hands folded, as a few practice taking mock blows without flinching

dialogue.text: For days, they drill not in swordplay but in stillness. To move towards violence and not answer it is a different kind of training.

panels.shot: medium shot of a smaller circle of women around Sarojini; one young woman speaks, anxious

dialogue.text: Women have already marched in cities, sold salt, courted arrest. Now, at Dharasana, they will be in the very front ranks.

panels.shot: pre-dawn wide shot: long line of satyagrahis on a dusty road, silhouettes against first light, Sarojini at the head

dialogue.text: On 21 May, they set out for the Dharasana Salt Works. No weapons, no helmets, only cotton cloth and a decision.

panels.shot: low wide shot from behind the satyagrahis as they approach the barbed-wire fence and a line of police with lathis

dialogue.text: Ahead lies the white crust of government salt and a ring of armed police. The British state will defend its monopoly with seasoned lathis.

panels.shot: medium shot of Sarojini and a British police officer facing each other across a few feet of dust

dialogue.speaker: sarojini_naidu
dialogue.text: We come only to take salt that the sea gives freely.

panels.shot: close-up on Sarojini’s hand raised slightly, signalling the first batch forward, police line tense in the background

dialogue.text: They approach in batches, kneeling at the fence. Each knows he may not stand up unaided.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-shot capturing the arc of a raised lathi and the calm, bowed head of the first satyagraha volunteer

dialogue.text: Then the lathis fall. Webb Miller will write of steel-tipped clubs smashing into unprotected shoulders and backs, again and again.

panels.shot: medium shot of Sarojini turned slightly away, eyes tightened but body steady as more blows fall in the background

dialogue.speaker: sarojini_naidu
dialogue.text: Remember, no cry for mercy. Let the world be our witness.

panels.shot: wide shot of the ground: rows of prone satyagrahis being carried away by comrades while another batch walks forward

dialogue.text: As each line crumples, another steps in. Miller counts men dropping in tens and dozens, some unconscious, some barely able to crawl.

panels.shot: close-up on a satyagrahi’s face as he grimaces, teeth clenched, yet does not raise an arm to defend himself

dialogue.text: He notes too that not one strike is returned. No stone flies, no fist is raised. This, he cables, is 'one of the most brutal and cold-blooded' scenes he has seen.

panels.shot: interior newsroom wide shot: editors crowded around a teleprinter as a clerk types, a strip of paper bearing Miller’s dispatch curling out

dialogue.text: British officials try to stop the story, but United Press cables it out. In America, in Europe, readers learn of unarmed Indians beaten at a salt depot.

panels.shot: formal wide shot of the United States Senate chamber, a senator standing, reading from a sheet as others listen

dialogue.text: In May 1930, Miller’s words are read into the United States Congressional Record. Dharasana enters the debates of another parliament, half a world away.

panels.shot: medium shot: back in camp, Sarojini sitting among injured volunteers, bandaged heads and shoulders around her

dialogue.text: Civil disobedience does not topple the Raj in a day. But historians will point to Dharasana as the moment when non-violence and modern communication fused into a new kind of power.

panels.shot: close-up on Sarojini looking out of frame, distant salt pans and a hazy horizon reflected in her eyes

dialogue.text: At Dharasana, a poet and politician turned suffering into witness. Her name reminds us that leadership can wear a sari, and that courage can echo louder than any blow.
